definition: Acquiesce means to go along with something without protesting.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word acquiesce. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know acquiesce should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Though she thought the mural's colors were wrong for the lobby, the painter acquiesced and mixed them as ordered.
To humor someone is much milder than to acquiesce — humoring plays along for a moment, mostly to keep the peace, while acquiesce means genuinely accepting a decision your own judgment still doubts.
Submit goes further than acquiesce — acquiescing swallows one decision; submitting hands over your will across the board.

Comply means doing what a rule or request says — neutral, paperwork-level obedience with no feeling attached either way. Acquiesce adds the swallowed objection: to acquiesce is to go along without protest while privately still disagreeing. You can comply cheerfully; nobody acquiesces cheerfully.

Capitulate means to stop resisting and give in, usually after open opposition and under real pressure — a besieged city, a holdout who finally folds. Acquiesce is quieter: there was never an open fight, only a doubt kept private while you go along.
to speak your disagreement out loud
to refuse openly and push back

Acquiesce means to go along with something without protesting.
The sous-chef believed the new tasting menu was too long.
He said so once, quietly; when the owner kept all nine courses, he acquiesced, tying his apron and working the line without another word.
Acquiesce is not plain agreement — it means going along without protest while your own doubts stay put.
The reluctance is the point: you accept the decision outwardly and keep the objection to yourself.
Acquiesce is the word for giving way without a fight — the objection is swallowed, not solved.
Reach for it when the reluctance matters.
Its unit-mates sit on either side: accede means granting a request, often after open resistance, and concede means admitting a point.
Only acquiesce insists on the silence.

When headquarters ordered the canyon trail rerouted along the sunny rim, ranger Tomás Ibarra thought at once of the August heat.
He drafted a memo about shade and water; he never sent it.
At the staff meeting he said nothing, and when the work order came he signed it and scheduled the crews.
Colleagues who knew his doubts asked why he chose to acquiesce rather than argue.
He shrugged: the decision had been made two levels above him, and he would live with it.
Privately, he still checks the heat readings every afternoon, and keeps the unsent memo in his desk.
